senses.gloss:
sthānaka
(‘standing [posture]’)
------------------------------------------
Images of deities installed in temples are generally of three types: स्थानक (standing), āsīna (sitting) and śayāna (reclining).
Images of the स्थानक type are the most common ones. These images can be samapāda (when the two feet are close together) or viṣamapāda (where one leg is straight and the other slightly bent and placed at a distance from the former).
See also MŪRTIŚILPAŚĀSTRA.

sthalapurāṇa
(‘local legend’)
------------------------------------------
Every place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, including its temples and sacred spots, has its own ancient story to tell. Such legends are transferred mostly by oral tradition, though the more famous ones have been incorporated in the well-known पुराणस् and उपपुराणस्. These are generally called sthalapurāṇas.
One of the interesting factors to be noted in such sthalapurāṇas is that some renowned personalities from the epics and the पुराणस् like राम, हनुमान् and कृष्ण, the Pāṇḍava brothers, sages like नारद, वसिष्ठ and अगस्त्य, or even great kings like विभीषण, प्रह्लाद and बलि will have visited almost all the places!

sthālīpāka
(‘boiling or cooking in the earthen pot’)
------------------------------------------
Sthālī is an earthen bowl used for holding rice grains.
When husked grains are cooked in the sthālī, on the दक्षिणाग्नि (See DAKṢIṆĀGNI.), mixed with clarified butter they form the स्थालीपाक. It is used as an oblation to the पितृस्.
It is also the name of a sacrifice belonging to the पाकयज्ञ group (See VEDIC SACRIFICES.). It is performed on the first full-मोओन् day after मर्रिअगे by the married couple. Its continued performance on the day of full-मोओन् and new-मोओन् throughout their lives has been recommended.

sthaṇḍila
------------------------------------------
The होम rites (See HOMA for details.) performed as a part of gṛhya or domestic religious ceremonies must always be performed on a स्थण्डिल.
A स्थण्डिल is a raised and perfectly levelled altar or platform of sand or loose earth raised by two or four finger breadths. It is a square measuring one iṣu (or length of an arrow i.e., 18 aṅgulas) on all sides. The measurement may be 21 or even 32 aṅgulas.
Lines—one horizontal and five vertical—are drawn as prescribed, on which the fire is placed.
The sacrificer sits facing the east, whereas the ब्रह्मा priest—the only priest in such rites—sits facing north.
